name: Browline glasses

lead: Browline glasses have a thick upper section that echoes the eyebrows, joined to thin metal (or clear) lower rims. For looksmaxxing the payoff is brow emphasis: the heavy top line draws attention to the brow and eye area and gives the upper face a stronger, more defined horizontal.

The style was introduced in 1947 by Shuron as the Ronsir and was reported to make up about half of all eyeglasses sold in the US in the 1950s. It returned in sunglasses in the 1980s and in eyeglasses in the 2010s, and Ray-Ban's Clubmaster is the best-known modern take.

paras: People choose browline frames in prescription or sunglass form, in acetate-and-metal or all-plastic builds, and in a range of lens sizes. Some wearers pick them to add presence over a lighter brow, others for a retro or professional look.

No health risks beyond ordinary eyewear fit and lens considerations. The look has carried changing social associations over the decades, from authority in the 1950s to stereotypes in the 1990s, and fit and lens size relative to face width affect how the frame reads.

angle.text: The heavy top bar echoes the eyebrows and sits where brow ridge definition reads on a face, so people use it to strengthen the look of the brow area while the slim lower rims keep the lower face unobstructed.

lead: Browline glasses are eyeglass frames whose thick upper portion, the brow bar, resembles eyebrows framing the eyes. The brows and temples are usually plastic and a metal chassis holds the bridge and eyewires.[1]

In looksmaxxing, they are used as a frame choice that adds visual weight across the brow line and the top of the eye area, in the way heavy brows do on a face. Users and style writers describe this as adding brow presence and a more defined upper face.
The design was introduced in 1947 by Jack Rohrbach of Shuron Ltd. as the Ronsir, built from interchangeable brows, bridges and eyewires.[1]
infobox: Acetate or plastic brow, metal lower rims[1]

paras: Standard browlines pair a plastic brow with a metal chassis; in the 1960s some models used aluminum brows. Monobrowlines, which join the bridge and brows into a single line, appeared in the 1980s and returned in the 2010s.[1] Later versions with clear plastic lower sections became a major style of their own.[1]
Shuron later added the rectangular Rondon to suit more face shapes.[1]

Jack Rohrbach of Shuron introduced the Ronsir in 1947, drawing on a British pre-war frame called the Supra.[1] In the 1950s browlines accounted for roughly half of all eyeglasses sold and worn, with wearers such as Malcolm X, Colonel Sanders and Lyndon B. Johnson.[1] Solid plastic frames overtook them in the 1960s, and Shuron sold its sixteen-millionth pair of Ronsirs in 1971.[1]

Browlines faded in the 1970s but resurfaced as sunglasses in the 1980s, boosted by Bruce Willis wearing tinted Ronsirs on Moonlighting; Ray-Ban's Clubmaster became the third best-selling sunglass style of that decade.[1] In the 1990s they carried associations with nerds and the elderly, then returned in the 2000s and 2010s with Mad Men and retro style, with Oakley leading monobrowline sales.[1]

Eyewear is discussed as a way to adjust the look of the brows and eye area without any procedure. Browline frames are cited for brow emphasis because the bar sits along the brow line.[2] Wearers also pick them for an older-style formal impression, a reputation the style carried in the 1950s.[2]
